column2: Monday morning. Yuna is too nervous to sleep before meeting Marc at ten. In the kitchen she asks Montse the time; Montse answers "son las ocho" and "tienes dos horas" (you have two hours) and tells her to stay calm, but does not offer to come along. Gentle, slightly tense.

column1: Sí, por favor. Montse… ¿Qué hora es?
column2: a little anxious, a beginner trying a new phrase
pointing at the wall clock, simple

In Marc's dim locksmith's workshop, full of stopped clocks, Marc lays Yuna's key beside the identical one from his window and finds it is not a door key but a clock key, for winding. His wristwatch has the same flower; it was his grandfather's, whose name is Martí: the "M." of the letters. Yuna uses "tengo" in answer to his "tienes". Marc is reserved and says little; Yuna is moved and short of Spanish. Quiet, growing realization.
careful, answering with the verb she just heard; stress "Tengo"

column1: No es una llave de puerta.

column2: honestly puzzled this time, not curt

Back at the boarding house, Yuna says Martí's name to Montse. Montse stops cutting, looks out of the window and only says it is hot, avoiding the question; after lunch she says they will go up to the park later, where there is wind. Tense, evasive.
evasive, looking out the window: not an answer

Late afternoon, Montse leads Yuna past the tourists of Park Güell to the hilltop with three crosses, overlooking Barcelona and the sea. Speaking very slowly so Yuna understands, Montse tells her that in 1978 Yuna's grandmother Sun-rye lived in her house for eight months and was her friend, and that Martí was Montse's brother. Montse tells the past in the present tense. Hushed and intimate; big revelations said simply.
a little dry, just between the two of them
out of breath, a beginner using "tengo"
slow and deliberate, so she understands
slow, remembering; the past told in the present tense
reading her first notebook entry written in Spanish, plain
